The second and the third terms are already bounded in Theorem~, and the first term relates to the training loss; we thereby utilize Theorem~ to finish the proof of the upper bounds. nodes.name: Proof sketch
nodes.statement: The training objective restricted to the parameter ball is a strongly convex quadratic in the linearization regime (kernel features are nearly fixed by Lemma~). Standard first-order oracle complexity (Nemirovski--Yudin lower bounds for quadratic minimization, see e.g.~citealpnes03) implies that no gradient-based method can decay the loss faster than exp(-Theta(sqrtlambdalambda_max)\,t) in continuous time, matching the discrete ((sqrtkappa-1)/(sqrtkappa+1))^2T bound after Tto t/eta with etato 0. Translating to compute via sf C=O(sf MTN) with sf M=Theta(sf N^3) and incorporating the 1/N factor in the rate (Remark~) recovers the exp(-Theta(sqrtkappa\,xi^2sf C/sf N^7)) rate. The full argument is in Appendix~.

Standard first-order oracle complexity (Nemirovski--Yudin lower bounds for quadratic minimization, see e.g.~\citealp{nes03}) implies that no gradient-based method can decay the loss faster than $\exp(-\Theta(\sqrt{\lambda\lambda_{\max}})\,t)$ in continuous time, matching the discrete $((\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1))^{2T}$ bound after $T\to t/\eta$ with $\eta\to 0$. The full argument is in Appendix~\ref{app_sub:lower_bounds}.

nodes.name: Cross-entropy vs.\ squared excess risk
nodes.statement: Cross-entropy after softmax shares its gradient form with squared loss in the logit space at the Bregman / natural-gradient level: with logits zinR^|V|, y'=softmax(z), and one-hot yinR^|V|, partial_z cal L_CE = y'-y which is the gradient of the Bregman divergence B_Phi^*(y, y') where Phi^* is the log-partition; this matches the squared-loss gradient z-y only in the well-specified, near-zero-excess regime (y'approx y, e.g.~CE near H(y)). For typical LM training (CE sim 1.5--2, far from H(y)), the two losses are not numerically identical even at the rate-exponent level, and our experiments are therefore meant to validate the qualitative predictions of Section~ (existence of the Stage~I/II transition; sf N^1/2-noise breakdown of data scaling) rather than the exact exponents.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem:ce_l2}
Cross-entropy after softmax shares its gradient form with squared loss in the logit space at the {\it Bregman / natural-gradient} level: with logits $z\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$, $y'={\rm softmax}(z)$, and one-hot $y\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$, $\partial_z {\cal L}_{\rm CE} = y'-y$ which is the gradient of the Bregman divergence $B_{\Phi^*}(y, y')$ where $\Phi^*$ is the log-partition; this matches the squared-loss gradient $z-y$ {\it only} in the well-specified, near-zero-excess regime ($y'\approx y$, e.g.~CE near $H(y)$). For typical LM training (CE $\sim 1.5$--$2$, far from $H(y)$), the two losses are not numerically identical even at the rate-exponent level, and our experiments are therefore meant to validate the {\it qualitative} predictions of Section~\ref{sec:scaling_law} (existence of the Stage~I/II transition; ${\sf N}^{1/2}$-noise breakdown of data scaling) rather than the exact exponents.

nodes.statement: We denote F^*: cal X to [C_1, C_2]^L times d as the target function (with F^*(X) bounded by fixed constants C_1, C_2inR). The input space cal X subseteq R^L times d is a combination of L d-dimensional balls where \|X_ell\|_2^2 = Theta(1), forall Xin cal X, ell in [L]. The data distribution is cal D = \(X, F^*(X)+Xi) : Xsim p_cal X,\, Xisim p_Xi\ subset cal X times R^Ltimes d where the noisy target Y = F^*(X)+Xi is unbounded in general. The random noise Xi in R^L times d is centred by 0_L times d and is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy xi^2: E[Xi] = 0_Ltimes d and max_ellin[L], kin[d] \|Xi_ell,k\|_psi_2^2 leq xi^2 (so E[exp(tXi_ell,k)] le exp(t^2xi^2/2)). The Gaussian case Xi_ell,ksimN(0,xi^2) used in the Le Cam statistical lower bound (Theorem~) is a special case. Only the noiseless target F^*(X) is bounded; the noisy target Y may take values outside [C_1, C_2]^Ltimes d, which is the natural setting under sub-Gaussian noise.

The input space ${\cal X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ is a combination of $L$ $d$-dimensional balls where $\|X_\ell\|_2^2 = \Theta(1), \forall X\in {\cal X}, \ell \in [L]$. The data distribution is ${\cal D} = \{(X, F^*(X)+\Xi) : X\sim p_{\cal X},\, \Xi\sim p_\Xi\} \subset {\cal X} \times \mathbb{R}^{L\times d}$ where the noisy target $Y = F^*(X)+\Xi$ is unbounded in general. The random noise $\Xi \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$ is centred by ${\bf 0}_{L \times d}$ and is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\xi^2$: ${\mathbb{E}}[\Xi] = {\bf 0}_{L\times d}$ and $\max_{\ell\in[L], k\in[d]} \|\Xi_{\ell,k}\|_{\psi_2}^2 \leq \xi^2$ (so ${\mathbb{E}}[\exp(t\Xi_{\ell,k})] \le \exp(t^2\xi^2/2)$). The Gaussian case $\Xi_{\ell,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\xi^2)$ used in the Le Cam statistical lower bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_stat}) is a special case. Only the noiseless target $F^*(X)$ is bounded; the noisy target $Y$ may take values outside $[C_1, C_2]^{L\times d}$, which is the natural setting under sub-Gaussian noise.

Assuming there exists a constant R in (0, 1) satisfying \| w_(nu), r(t) - w_(nu), r(0) \|_2 leq R and \| U_(nu)(t) - U_(nu)(0)\|_F leq R for r in [m] and nu in [N] and R in (0, 1). We mark the indices as: rin [m], p in [nL], ell_1, ell_2 in [L], and nu in [N]. We denote i = lfloor p / L rfloor, ell = p ~ mod~ L, ell' in [ell]. If Definition~ holds, then with a probability at least 1 - delta, we have: item Basic Bounds. item Part 1. \| w_(nu), r(0) \|_2 leq O(sqrtdB). item Part 2. \| U_(nu)(0) \|_F leq O(dB). item Part 3. \| w_(nu), r(t) \|_2 leq O(sqrtdB). item Part 4. \| U_(nu)(t) \|_F leq O(dB). item Part 5. \| Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t) \|_2 = Theta(1) for all ell in [L]. item Part 6. \| Lambda_(nu), i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i(t)^top \|_infty leq O(dB). item Part 7. expbig( [Lambda_(nu), i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i(t)^top]_ell_1, ell_2 big) in [ exp(-O(dB)), exp(O(dB)) ] for all ell_1, ell_2 in [L]. item Part 8. nodes.statement: Proof of Part 1. Each entry w_(nu),r,k(0) is i.i.d.\ N(0,1) by initialization. By Fact~, |w_(nu),r,k(0)| le Csqrtlog(Nmd/delta) with probability at least 1 - delta/(Nmd). A union bound over nuin[N], rin[m], kin[d] shows that all entries are bounded by Csqrtlog(Nmd/delta) simultaneously with probability at least 1-delta. Thus \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2^2 = sum_kin[d] w_(nu),r,k(0)^2 le d cdot C^2log(Nmd/delta) = O(d B^2), giving \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt d B). Proof of Part 2. Analogously, each entry U_(nu),k_1,k_2(0) is i.i.d.\ N(0,1). By Fact~ and a union bound over nuin[N], (k_1,k_2)in[d]times[d], all entries are bounded by O(B) with probability at least 1-delta. Therefore \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F^2 = sum_k_1,k_2 U_(nu),k_1,k_2(0)^2 le d^2cdot O(B^2) = O(d^2 B^2), hence \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F le O(dB). Proof of Part 3. By triangle inequality, \|w_(nu),r(t)\|_2 le \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 + \|w_(nu),r(t)-w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt dB) + R from Part~1 and the lemma's hypothesis. Since R in (0,1) and Bge 1 (so sqrt d Bge 1), the second summand is dominated and \|w_(nu),r(t)\|_2 le O(sqrt d B). Proof of Part 4. Analogously to Part~3, \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F le \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F + \|U_(nu)(t)-U_(nu)(0)\|_F le O(dB) + R, and the second summand is dominated by the first under Rin(0,1) and Bge 1, giving \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F le O(dB). Proof of Part 5. Because A_(nu) is trained jointly with W_(nu),U_(nu) by gradient flow (Section~), the entries a_(nu),r,k(t) are no longer in \-1,+1\ for t>0 and are in general not independent of w_(nu),r(t). We therefore prove Part~5 in two steps: first at the initialization time t=0 via Hoeffding (where the i.i.d.\ pm 1 assumption holds), then for t>0 via the perturbation bound of Part~13 of this lemma and the FFN-drift bound of Lemma~. Step 1: nu=1 at t=0. The data assumption (Section~) gives \|Lambda_(0), i, ell\|_2 = \|X_i,ell+E_ell\|_2 = Theta(1) for every ell. Combined with the fact that sigma_(1), p(0) is a probability vector, \|o_(1), p(0)\|_2 = \|Lambda_(0), i(0)^top sigma_(1), p(0)\|_2 le max_ell' \|Lambda_(0), i, ell'\|_2 = Theta(1). For the mu-term at t=0, we note that a_(1),r,k(0) in \-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ uniform and independent of w_(1),r(0)simN(0,I_d) (the i.i.d.\ initialization ensures this). Hence, fixing kin[d] and conditioning on w_(1),r(0): |a_(1), r, k(0)cdotphi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)| & ~ le 1cdot\|w_(1),r(0)\|_2cdot\|o_(1),p(0)\|_2 le O(sqrtdB), \\ Ebig[a_(1), r, k(0)cdotphi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)\,big|\, w_(1),r(0)big] & ~ = E[a_(1),r,k(0)]cdot phi(cdot) = 0. By Hoeffding (Lemma~) applied to sum_r=1^m a_(1),r,k(0)phi(langle o_(1),p(0),w_(1),r(0)rangle), with probability at least 1-delta/(md): Big|sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k(0)phi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)Big| le O(sqrtmdB)sqrtlog(md/delta) le O(sqrtm\,sqrtd\,B^2). Taking the union bound over kin[d]: \|mu_(1), p(0)\|_2 le fracomegasqrt dsqrt mmax_kin[d]Big|sum_r a_(1),r,k(0)phi(cdot)Big| le O(omega\, d\, B^2), and therefore \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 le \|Lambda_(0), i, ell(0)\|_2 + \|mu_(1), p(0)\|_2 le Theta(1) + O(omega d B^2) = Theta(1)pm o(1/N), where the last step uses omega = o(1/(NdB^2)) from Definition~. Step 2: Extension from t=0 to t>0. By Parts~9, 10 and~13 of this lemma (proven below), \|w_(1),r(t)-w_(1),r(0)\|_2 le R and \|o_(1),p(t)-o_(1),p(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt L R). By Lemma~, \|A_(nu)(t) - A_(nu)(0)\|_F le R_A := O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)). The Lipschitz expansion of the layer-1 hidden state with respect to (W,A,o) then gives: \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 &le fracomegasqrt m\,Big( \|A_(1)(t) - A_(1)(0)\|_Fcdot max_r |phi(langle w_(1),r(t),o_(1),p(t)rangle)| \\ & + \|A_(1)(0)\|_Fcdot big[max_r \|w_(1),r(t)-w_(1),r(0)\|_2cdot \|o_(1),p(t)\|_2 + cdotsbig]Big) \\ &le fracomegasqrt mbig( R_Acdot O(sqrt d B) + O(sqrtmd)cdot O(R) big) \\ &= OBig(fracomegasqrt d Bsqrt m\,omegalambda NBig) + O(omegasqrt d\, R) = o(1) under the strengthened width condition of Lemma~. Combining with Step~1: \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t)\|_2 le \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 + o(1) = Theta(1). Step 3: Inductive step (nu ge 2). Assume the bound holds for layer nu-1. Then \|Lambda_(nu-1),i,ell(t)\|_2 = Theta(1) uniformly in ell and t, hence \|o_(nu),p(t)\|_2 = \|Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)^topsigma_(nu),p(t)\|_2 le max_ell'\|Lambda_(nu-1),i,ell'(t)\|_2 = Theta(1). The Hoeffding-then-perturb argument of Steps~1 and~2 applies verbatim to mu_(nu),p (with all quantities re-indexed to layer nu), giving \|Lambda_(nu),i,ell(t)\|_2 = Theta(1) as claimed. The bound on \|o_(nu),p(t)\|_2 follows directly: \|o_(nu), p(t)\|_2 = Theta(1). Proof of Part 6. We have: \| Lambda_(nu), i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i(t)^top \|_infty = & ~ max_(ell_1, ell_2) in [L] times [L] left| Lambda_(nu), i, ell_1(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell_2(t) right| \\ leq & ~ O(dB) where the first step follows from simple algebra, the second step follows from Part 4 and Part 5 of this lemma and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Proof of Part 7. From Part~6, \|Lambda_(nu),i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu),i(t)^top\|_infty le O(dB), so each attention logit z_p,ell' := big[Lambda_(nu),i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu),i(t)^topbig]_ell, ell' satisfies |z_p,ell'| le O(dB). Therefore exp(z_p,ell') in [exp(-O(dB)), exp(O(dB))], which is the claim. Proof of Part 8. Following Part 7 of this lemma, we can show that: sum_ell'in [ell] exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) le ell exp(O(dB)) le L exp(O(dB)). Then we can show that: sigma_(nu), p, ell'(t) ge & ~ exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) / sum_ell'in [ell] exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) \\ ge & ~ fracexp(-O(dB))L exp(O(dB)) \\ ge & ~ fracexp(-O(dB))L. Combining the previous results, we obtain the result of this part. Proof of Part 9. This is a direct restatement of the lemma's hypothesis \|w_(nu),r(t) - w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le R, which is a bootstrapping assumption that is verified self-consistently in Lemma~ (where we prove that the gradient flow keeps the iterates inside this ball). Proof of Part 10. Likewise, this is a direct restatement of the hypothesis \|U_(nu)(t) - U_(nu)(0)\|_F le R, verified self-consistently in Lemma~. Proof of Part 11, 12 and 13. We proceed by induction on the layer index nu. The base case nu=0 is trivial since Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) = X_i,ell + E_ell does not depend on t, and so Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) = Lambda_(0), i, ell(0). Base case: nu=1. By the definition of Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) as the ell-th token of layer-1 output: & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 \\ = & ~ sqrtsum_kin [d] left(fracomegasqrtm cdot sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k left(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle) right) right)^2 , where the residual connection contributes Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) = 0 and the difference reduces to the FFN-after-attention contribution. We first bound \|sigma_(1),p(t)-sigma_(1),p(0)\|_2 via softmax Lipschitzness. Note that sigma_(1),p(t) is a function of the attention logits Lambda_(0), i(0) U_(1)(t)^top Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) in R^L (here Lambda_(0), i(t)=Lambda_(0), i(0) is fixed). Hence: \| sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) \|_2 leq & ~ O(1) cdot \| Lambda_(0), i(0) ( U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0) )^top Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_F cdot \| U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0) \|_F cdot \| Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot O(sqrtL) cdot R cdot O(1) = O(sqrtLR), where the first step follows from the definition of sigma_(1), p(t) and Fact~, the second step from operator-norm submultiplicativity (Cauchy--Schwarz on a quadratic form), the third step from \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_F = O(sqrtL) (since each token has unit norm, summed over L tokens), \|U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0)\|_F le R (Part 10), and \|Lambda_(0), i, ell(0)\|_2 = O(1). Next, we use the identity o_(1),p(t) = Lambda_(0), i(0)^top sigma_(1), p(t) together with the operator-norm bound \|Lambda_(0),i(0)\|_op = O(1) that follows from the per-token unit-norm constraint \|X_ell\|_2 = Theta(1) (Section~) under the residual-and-RMSNorm structure: \| o_(1), p(t) - o_(1), p(0) \|_2 = & ~ \| Lambda_(0), i(0)^top big( sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) big) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_op cdot \| sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot O(sqrtLR) = O(sqrtL R), which matches Part~13. For a fixed index k in [d], we apply Hoeffding's inequality (Lemma~) to the random variables a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) for r in [m]. By Fact~ (the ReLU phi is 1-Lipschitz): & ~ big| a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) big| \\ leq & ~ |a_(1), r, k| cdot big| langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle - langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle big| \\ leq & ~ 1 cdot big( \| w_(1), r(t) - w_(1), r(0) \|_2 cdot \| o_(1), p(t) \|_2 + \| w_(1), r(0) \|_2 cdot \| o_(1), p(t) - o_(1), p(0) \|_2 big) \\ leq & ~ R cdot O(1) + O(sqrtd B) cdot O(sqrtL R) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLdBR), where the second step follows from |a_(1),r,k|=1 and the bilinear difference identity, the third step from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality together with the perturbation bounds Part 9 and Part 13 of this lemma, the fourth step from \|w_(1),r(0)\|_2leq O(sqrtdB) (Part 1) and \|o_(1),p(t)\|_2 = O(1). The mean is zero since a_(1), r, k in \-1,+1\ uniformly and is independent of w: Ebig[a_(1), r, k cdot big( phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big)big] = 0. By Lemma~, for any fixed k, with probability at least 1 - delta/(md): & ~ Big| fracomegasqrtm sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) Big| \\ & leq fracomegasqrtmcdot O(sqrtLdBR)cdotsqrtmlog(md/delta) \\ & leq OBig(omega sqrtLdBRcdot BBig) = Obig(omega sqrtLdB^2Rbig). Choosing omega = o(1/(NL^2d^2.5B^3)) as in Definition~, this is bounded by O(R/(BdsqrtLd)), which is dominated by R. We therefore get \| Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0) \|_2 leq O(R) for all ell in [ell] and \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_infty leq O(R/sqrtd). When nu=2, we have: & ~ \|sigma_(2), p (t) - sigma_(2), p (0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot \| Lambda_(1), i(t) U_(2)(t)^top Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0) U_(2)(0)^top Lambda_(1), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ = & ~ O(1) cdot \| (Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t))^top vec( U_(2)(t)) - (Lambda_(1), i(0) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(0))^top vec( U_(2)(0))\|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot Big( \|Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t)\|_F cdot O(R) \\ & ~ ~~~~~~~~~~~~+\| U_(2)(0) \|_F cdot \| Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_FBig) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLR) where the first step follows from simple algebra and Fact~, the second step follows from a basic tensor trick, the third step follows from the sum form of the triangle inequality \|AB - A'B'\|_F le \|A-A'\|_F \|B\|_F + \|A'\|_F \|B-B'\|_F together with Part 4 of this lemma and \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_infty leq O(R/(BdsqrtLd)). Hence, we have: \| o_(2), i(t) - o_(2), i(0) \|_2 = & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i(t)^top sigma_(2), p(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0)^top sigma_(2), p(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0)\|_F cdot \|sigma_(2),p(t)\|_2 + \| Lambda_(1), i(0)\|_op cdot \|sigma_(2),p(t)-sigma_(2),p(0)\|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(sqrt L R)cdot O(1) + O(1)cdot O(sqrtLR) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLR), where these steps follow from the sum triangle inequality \|AB-A'B'\|le \|A-A'\|\|B\| + \|A'\|\|B-B'\|, Fact~ for the softmax bound, and Part 10 of this Lemma. To extend \|Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0)\|_2 from a nu=2-specific bound to the inductive step, we apply the same two-step argument as in Part~5. At t=0, a_(2),r,k(0)in\-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ uniform and independent of w_(2),r(0), so Hoeffding's inequality (Lemma~) bounds the i.i.d.\ component as O(sqrtmsqrtdB^2) with high probability; for t>0, the difference Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0) contains contributions from w_(2), U_(2), A_(2) drift, each bounded by R, R, R_A respectively (from Parts~9, 10 of this lemma and Lemma~). The Lipschitz expansion in (W, U, A) yields: \|Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt L R) + O(omega sqrt d B cdot R_A) = O(sqrt L R), where the second equality uses the strengthened width condition of Lemma~ so that the A-drift term is dominated by the W,U-drift. By induction (using the same two-step Hoeffding-then-perturb argument at each layer), we obtain the bounds of Parts~11, 12, and 13. Proof of Part 14. We have: cal L(t, D) = & ~ frac1n \| sf F(t) - sf Y \|_F^2 \\ leq & ~ Lmax_p in [nL] \| sf F_p(t) - sf Y_p \|_2^2 \\ leq & ~ Lmax_p in [nL] left( \| sf F_p(t)\|_2 + \| sf Y_p \|_2 right)^2 \\ leq & ~ L left( O(1) + O(sqrtd) right)^2 \\ leq & ~ O(Ld), where the first step follows from Lemma~, the second step follows from simple algebras, the third step follows from the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, the last two steps follow from Definition~ and simple algebras. Proof of Part 15. We show that \|fracd cal L(t,D)dmu_(nu)(t)\|_F^2 asymp fracvarepsilon^2n cdot cal L(t,D) by reverse induction on nu from N down to 1. The 1/n factor in the bound is essential and traceable to the 1/n in the definition L = frac1n\|F-Y\|_F^2 of the average training loss (see the base case below). Base case: nu = N. By Part 3 of Lemma~, fracdcal L(t,D)d mu_(N), p(t) = frac2varepsilonn(sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p) since G_(N),p(t) = 0_d. Hence: Big\|fracdcal L(t,D)d mu_(N)(t)Big\|_F^2 = frac4varepsilon^2n^2sum_p \|sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p\|_2^2 = frac4varepsilon^2ncdot cal L(t,D), using sum_p \|F_p-Y_p\|_2^2 = n\,L(t,D) from Lemma~. This establishes \|fracdcal Ldmu_(N)\|_F^2 le 4varepsilon^2 L/n le O(varepsilon^2 Ld/n) via Part~14, hence \|fracdcal Ldmu_(N)\|_F le O(varepsilonsqrtLd/n). Inductive step. Assume the claim for layer nu+1. We bound the auxiliary term G_(nu),p(t) (Part~3 of Lemma~). The factor kappa U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)^top diag(1_n - frac12e_ell) (diagsigma - sigmasigma^top)Lambda_(nu-1),i(t) is bounded by: & ~ big\| kappa U_(nu)(t)Lambda_(nu-1), i (t)^top diag(1_n - tfrac12e_ell) (diagsigma_(nu), p(t) - sigma_(nu), p(t)sigma_(nu), p(t)^top)Lambda_(nu-1), i (t) big\|_F \\ leq & ~ kappa cdot \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F cdot \|Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)\|_F^2 cdot O(1) \\ leq & ~ kappa cdot O(dB) cdot O(L) cdot O(1) \\ = & ~ O(kappa L^2dB) leq O(L^2dB), where we use Parts 4 and 5, the fact that diagsigma - sigmasigma^top has spectral norm at most 1, and kappa = 1/sqrtm leq 1. To bound the random sum sum_rin[m] a_(nu),r(t)langlefracdcal Ldmu_(nu+1),p, a_(nu),r(t)rangle\, w_(nu),r(t)\,I\cdot\, we again apply Hoeffding at t=0 (where a_(nu),r,k(0)in\-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ and independent of w_(nu),r(0)) to obtain \|G_(nu),p(0)\|_2^2 le omegacdot O(L^2 d^2.5 B^3), and then propagate to t>0 via the A-drift bound \|A_(nu)(t)-A_(nu)(0)\|_F le R_A from Lemma~ and the W-drift bound \|w_(nu),r(t)-w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le R from Part~9 of this lemma: \|G_(nu),p(t)\|_2 le \|G_(nu),p(0)\|_2 + O(omegasqrtm\,\|A_(nu)(t)-A_(nu)(0)\|_F + omegasqrtm d\,R) = O(sqrtomega cdot Ld^1.25B^1.5), so that \|G_(nu),p(t)\|_2^2 le omegacdot O(L^2 d^2.5B^3) le o(1) under Definition~'s choice omega = o(1/(NL^2 d^2.5B^3)) and the strengthened width of Lemma~. Therefore I_d + diag(G_(nu),p(t)) = (1pm o(1))I_d, and by Part~3 of Lemma~: Big\|fracdcal Ldmu_(nu),p(t)Big\|_2 = frac2varepsilonn\|(sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p)\|_2(1pm o(1)), which preserves the Theta(varepsilon^2cal L/n) per-layer scaling. Summing over pin[nL] (which produces a single factor of n from sum_p \|F_p-Y_p\|^2 = nL) and inducting: big\| fracd cal L(t, D)d mu_(nu)(t) big\|_F^2 asymp fracvarepsilon^2n cdot cal L(t, D). Proof of Part 16. We bound \|gamma_(nu),p(t)\|_2, where gamma_(nu),p(t) is the kernel feature for U_(nu). By the definition, the leading factor is fracomega kappasqrtm, multiplied by tensors of bounded norm (Part~5, Part~7) and a sum over r that is controlled by Hoeffding as in Part~15. Choosing kappa = 1/sqrtm as in Definition~, we have fracomegakappasqrtm = fracomegam, and the entire bound reduces to \| gamma_(nu),p(t)\|_2 leq o(1/sqrtm), completing the proof. This completes the proof of all parts of the lemma.

A union bound over nuin[N], rin[m], kin[d] shows that all entries are bounded by Csqrtlog(Nmd/delta) simultaneously with probability at least 1-delta. Thus \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2^2 = sum_kin[d] w_(nu),r,k(0)^2 le d cdot C^2log(Nmd/delta) = O(d B^2), giving \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt d B). Proof of Part 2. Analogously, each entry U_(nu),k_1,k_2(0) is i.i.d.\ N(0,1). By Fact~ and a union bound over nuin[N], (k_1,k_2)in[d]times[d], all entries are bounded by O(B) with probability at least 1-delta. Therefore \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F^2 = sum_k_1,k_2 U_(nu),k_1,k_2(0)^2 le d^2cdot O(B^2) = O(d^2 B^2), hence \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F le O(dB). Proof of Part 3. By triangle inequality, \|w_(nu),r(t)\|_2 le \|w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 + \|w_(nu),r(t)-w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt dB) + R from Part~1 and the lemma's hypothesis. Since R in (0,1) and Bge 1 (so sqrt d Bge 1), the second summand is dominated and \|w_(nu),r(t)\|_2 le O(sqrt d B). Proof of Part 4. Analogously to Part~3, \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F le \|U_(nu)(0)\|_F + \|U_(nu)(t)-U_(nu)(0)\|_F le O(dB) + R, and the second summand is dominated by the first under Rin(0,1) and Bge 1, giving \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F le O(dB). Proof of Part 5. Because A_(nu) is trained jointly with W_(nu),U_(nu) by gradient flow (Section~), the entries a_(nu),r,k(t) are no longer in \-1,+1\ for t>0 and are in general not independent of w_(nu),r(t). We therefore prove Part~5 in two steps: first at the initialization time t=0 via Hoeffding (where the i.i.d.\ pm 1 assumption holds), then for t>0 via the perturbation bound of Part~13 of this lemma and the FFN-drift bound of Lemma~. Step 1: nu=1 at t=0. The data assumption (Section~) gives \|Lambda_(0), i, ell\|_2 = \|X_i,ell+E_ell\|_2 = Theta(1) for every ell. Combined with the fact that sigma_(1), p(0) is a probability vector, \|o_(1), p(0)\|_2 = \|Lambda_(0), i(0)^top sigma_(1), p(0)\|_2 le max_ell' \|Lambda_(0), i, ell'\|_2 = Theta(1). For the mu-term at t=0, we note that a_(1),r,k(0) in \-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ uniform and independent of w_(1),r(0)simN(0,I_d) (the i.i.d.\ initialization ensures this). Hence, fixing kin[d] and conditioning on w_(1),r(0): |a_(1), r, k(0)cdotphi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)| & ~ le 1cdot\|w_(1),r(0)\|_2cdot\|o_(1),p(0)\|_2 le O(sqrtdB), \\ Ebig[a_(1), r, k(0)cdotphi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)\,big|\, w_(1),r(0)big] & ~ = E[a_(1),r,k(0)]cdot phi(cdot) = 0. By Hoeffding (Lemma~) applied to sum_r=1^m a_(1),r,k(0)phi(langle o_(1),p(0),w_(1),r(0)rangle), with probability at least 1-delta/(md): Big|sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k(0)phi(langle o_(1), p(0), w_(1), r(0)rangle)Big| le O(sqrtmdB)sqrtlog(md/delta) le O(sqrtm\,sqrtd\,B^2). Taking the union bound over kin[d]: \|mu_(1), p(0)\|_2 le fracomegasqrt dsqrt mmax_kin[d]Big|sum_r a_(1),r,k(0)phi(cdot)Big| le O(omega\, d\, B^2), and therefore \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 le \|Lambda_(0), i, ell(0)\|_2 + \|mu_(1), p(0)\|_2 le Theta(1) + O(omega d B^2) = Theta(1)pm o(1/N), where the last step uses omega = o(1/(NdB^2)) from Definition~. Step 2: Extension from t=0 to t>0. By Parts~9, 10 and~13 of this lemma (proven below), \|w_(1),r(t)-w_(1),r(0)\|_2 le R and \|o_(1),p(t)-o_(1),p(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt L R). By Lemma~, \|A_(nu)(t) - A_(nu)(0)\|_F le R_A := O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)). The Lipschitz expansion of the layer-1 hidden state with respect to (W,A,o) then gives: \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 &le fracomegasqrt m\,Big( \|A_(1)(t) - A_(1)(0)\|_Fcdot max_r |phi(langle w_(1),r(t),o_(1),p(t)rangle)| \\ & + \|A_(1)(0)\|_Fcdot big[max_r \|w_(1),r(t)-w_(1),r(0)\|_2cdot \|o_(1),p(t)\|_2 + cdotsbig]Big) \\ &le fracomegasqrt mbig( R_Acdot O(sqrt d B) + O(sqrtmd)cdot O(R) big) \\ &= OBig(fracomegasqrt d Bsqrt m\,omegalambda NBig) + O(omegasqrt d\, R) = o(1) under the strengthened width condition of Lemma~. Combining with Step~1: \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t)\|_2 le \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 + o(1) = Theta(1). Step 3: Inductive step (nu ge 2). Assume the bound holds for layer nu-1. Then \|Lambda_(nu-1),i,ell(t)\|_2 = Theta(1) uniformly in ell and t, hence \|o_(nu),p(t)\|_2 = \|Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)^topsigma_(nu),p(t)\|_2 le max_ell'\|Lambda_(nu-1),i,ell'(t)\|_2 = Theta(1). The Hoeffding-then-perturb argument of Steps~1 and~2 applies verbatim to mu_(nu),p (with all quantities re-indexed to layer nu), giving \|Lambda_(nu),i,ell(t)\|_2 = Theta(1) as claimed. The bound on \|o_(nu),p(t)\|_2 follows directly: \|o_(nu), p(t)\|_2 = Theta(1). Proof of Part 6. We have: \| Lambda_(nu), i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i(t)^top \|_infty = & ~ max_(ell_1, ell_2) in [L] times [L] left| Lambda_(nu), i, ell_1(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell_2(t) right| \\ leq & ~ O(dB) where the first step follows from simple algebra, the second step follows from Part 4 and Part 5 of this lemma and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Proof of Part 7. From Part~6, \|Lambda_(nu),i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu),i(t)^top\|_infty le O(dB), so each attention logit z_p,ell' := big[Lambda_(nu),i(t) U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu),i(t)^topbig]_ell, ell' satisfies |z_p,ell'| le O(dB). Therefore exp(z_p,ell') in [exp(-O(dB)), exp(O(dB))], which is the claim. Proof of Part 8. Following Part 7 of this lemma, we can show that: sum_ell'in [ell] exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) le ell exp(O(dB)) le L exp(O(dB)). Then we can show that: sigma_(nu), p, ell'(t) ge & ~ exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) / sum_ell'in [ell] exp(Lambda_(nu), i, ell(t)^top U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu), i, ell'(t)) \\ ge & ~ fracexp(-O(dB))L exp(O(dB)) \\ ge & ~ fracexp(-O(dB))L. Combining the previous results, we obtain the result of this part. Proof of Part 9. This is a direct restatement of the lemma's hypothesis \|w_(nu),r(t) - w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le R, which is a bootstrapping assumption that is verified self-consistently in Lemma~ (where we prove that the gradient flow keeps the iterates inside this ball). Proof of Part 10. Likewise, this is a direct restatement of the hypothesis \|U_(nu)(t) - U_(nu)(0)\|_F le R, verified self-consistently in Lemma~. Proof of Part 11, 12 and 13. We proceed by induction on the layer index nu. The base case nu=0 is trivial since Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) = X_i,ell + E_ell does not depend on t, and so Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) = Lambda_(0), i, ell(0). Base case: nu=1. By the definition of Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) as the ell-th token of layer-1 output: & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_2 \\ = & ~ sqrtsum_kin [d] left(fracomegasqrtm cdot sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k left(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle) right) right)^2 , where the residual connection contributes Lambda_(0), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) = 0 and the difference reduces to the FFN-after-attention contribution. We first bound \|sigma_(1),p(t)-sigma_(1),p(0)\|_2 via softmax Lipschitzness. Note that sigma_(1),p(t) is a function of the attention logits Lambda_(0), i(0) U_(1)(t)^top Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) in R^L (here Lambda_(0), i(t)=Lambda_(0), i(0) is fixed). Hence: \| sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) \|_2 leq & ~ O(1) cdot \| Lambda_(0), i(0) ( U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0) )^top Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_F cdot \| U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0) \|_F cdot \| Lambda_(0), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot O(sqrtL) cdot R cdot O(1) = O(sqrtLR), where the first step follows from the definition of sigma_(1), p(t) and Fact~, the second step from operator-norm submultiplicativity (Cauchy--Schwarz on a quadratic form), the third step from \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_F = O(sqrtL) (since each token has unit norm, summed over L tokens), \|U_(1)(t) - U_(1)(0)\|_F le R (Part 10), and \|Lambda_(0), i, ell(0)\|_2 = O(1). Next, we use the identity o_(1),p(t) = Lambda_(0), i(0)^top sigma_(1), p(t) together with the operator-norm bound \|Lambda_(0),i(0)\|_op = O(1) that follows from the per-token unit-norm constraint \|X_ell\|_2 = Theta(1) (Section~) under the residual-and-RMSNorm structure: \| o_(1), p(t) - o_(1), p(0) \|_2 = & ~ \| Lambda_(0), i(0)^top big( sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) big) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ \|Lambda_(0), i(0)\|_op cdot \| sigma_(1), p(t) - sigma_(1), p(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot O(sqrtLR) = O(sqrtL R), which matches Part~13. For a fixed index k in [d], we apply Hoeffding's inequality (Lemma~) to the random variables a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) for r in [m]. By Fact~ (the ReLU phi is 1-Lipschitz): & ~ big| a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) big| \\ leq & ~ |a_(1), r, k| cdot big| langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle - langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle big| \\ leq & ~ 1 cdot big( \| w_(1), r(t) - w_(1), r(0) \|_2 cdot \| o_(1), p(t) \|_2 + \| w_(1), r(0) \|_2 cdot \| o_(1), p(t) - o_(1), p(0) \|_2 big) \\ leq & ~ R cdot O(1) + O(sqrtd B) cdot O(sqrtL R) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLdBR), where the second step follows from |a_(1),r,k|=1 and the bilinear difference identity, the third step from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality together with the perturbation bounds Part 9 and Part 13 of this lemma, the fourth step from \|w_(1),r(0)\|_2leq O(sqrtdB) (Part 1) and \|o_(1),p(t)\|_2 = O(1). The mean is zero since a_(1), r, k in \-1,+1\ uniformly and is independent of w: Ebig[a_(1), r, k cdot big( phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big)big] = 0. By Lemma~, for any fixed k, with probability at least 1 - delta/(md): & ~ Big| fracomegasqrtm sum_r=1^m a_(1), r, k cdot big(phi(langle w_(1), r(t), o_(1), p(t) rangle) - phi(langle w_(1), r(0), o_(1), p(0) rangle)big) Big| \\ & leq fracomegasqrtmcdot O(sqrtLdBR)cdotsqrtmlog(md/delta) \\ & leq OBig(omega sqrtLdBRcdot BBig) = Obig(omega sqrtLdB^2Rbig). Choosing omega = o(1/(NL^2d^2.5B^3)) as in Definition~, this is bounded by O(R/(BdsqrtLd)), which is dominated by R. We therefore get \| Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0) \|_2 leq O(R) for all ell in [ell] and \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_infty leq O(R/sqrtd). When nu=2, we have: & ~ \|sigma_(2), p (t) - sigma_(2), p (0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot \| Lambda_(1), i(t) U_(2)(t)^top Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0) U_(2)(0)^top Lambda_(1), i, ell(0) \|_2 \\ = & ~ O(1) cdot \| (Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t))^top vec( U_(2)(t)) - (Lambda_(1), i(0) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(0))^top vec( U_(2)(0))\|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(1) cdot Big( \|Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t)\|_F cdot O(R) \\ & ~ ~~~~~~~~~~~~+\| U_(2)(0) \|_F cdot \| Lambda_(1), i(t) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0) otimes Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_FBig) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLR) where the first step follows from simple algebra and Fact~, the second step follows from a basic tensor trick, the third step follows from the sum form of the triangle inequality \|AB - A'B'\|_F le \|A-A'\|_F \|B\|_F + \|A'\|_F \|B-B'\|_F together with Part 4 of this lemma and \|Lambda_(1), i, ell(t) -Lambda_(1), i, ell(0)\|_infty leq O(R/(BdsqrtLd)). Hence, we have: \| o_(2), i(t) - o_(2), i(0) \|_2 = & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i(t)^top sigma_(2), p(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0)^top sigma_(2), p(0) \|_2 \\ leq & ~ \| Lambda_(1), i(t) - Lambda_(1), i(0)\|_F cdot \|sigma_(2),p(t)\|_2 + \| Lambda_(1), i(0)\|_op cdot \|sigma_(2),p(t)-sigma_(2),p(0)\|_2 \\ leq & ~ O(sqrt L R)cdot O(1) + O(1)cdot O(sqrtLR) \\ leq & ~ O(sqrtLR), where these steps follow from the sum triangle inequality \|AB-A'B'\|le \|A-A'\|\|B\| + \|A'\|\|B-B'\|, Fact~ for the softmax bound, and Part 10 of this Lemma. To extend \|Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0)\|_2 from a nu=2-specific bound to the inductive step, we apply the same two-step argument as in Part~5. At t=0, a_(2),r,k(0)in\-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ uniform and independent of w_(2),r(0), so Hoeffding's inequality (Lemma~) bounds the i.i.d.\ component as O(sqrtmsqrtdB^2) with high probability; for t>0, the difference Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0) contains contributions from w_(2), U_(2), A_(2) drift, each bounded by R, R, R_A respectively (from Parts~9, 10 of this lemma and Lemma~). The Lipschitz expansion in (W, U, A) yields: \|Lambda_(2),i,ell(t)-Lambda_(2),i,ell(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt L R) + O(omega sqrt d B cdot R_A) = O(sqrt L R), where the second equality uses the strengthened width condition of Lemma~ so that the A-drift term is dominated by the W,U-drift. By induction (using the same two-step Hoeffding-then-perturb argument at each layer), we obtain the bounds of Parts~11, 12, and 13. Proof of Part 14. We have: cal L(t, D) = & ~ frac1n \| sf F(t) - sf Y \|_F^2 \\ leq & ~ Lmax_p in [nL] \| sf F_p(t) - sf Y_p \|_2^2 \\ leq & ~ Lmax_p in [nL] left( \| sf F_p(t)\|_2 + \| sf Y_p \|_2 right)^2 \\ leq & ~ L left( O(1) + O(sqrtd) right)^2 \\ leq & ~ O(Ld), where the first step follows from Lemma~, the second step follows from simple algebras, the third step follows from the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, the last two steps follow from Definition~ and simple algebras. Proof of Part 15. We show that \|fracd cal L(t,D)dmu_(nu)(t)\|_F^2 asymp fracvarepsilon^2n cdot cal L(t,D) by reverse induction on nu from N down to 1. The 1/n factor in the bound is essential and traceable to the 1/n in the definition L = frac1n\|F-Y\|_F^2 of the average training loss (see the base case below). Base case: nu = N. By Part 3 of Lemma~, fracdcal L(t,D)d mu_(N), p(t) = frac2varepsilonn(sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p) since G_(N),p(t) = 0_d. Hence: Big\|fracdcal L(t,D)d mu_(N)(t)Big\|_F^2 = frac4varepsilon^2n^2sum_p \|sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p\|_2^2 = frac4varepsilon^2ncdot cal L(t,D), using sum_p \|F_p-Y_p\|_2^2 = n\,L(t,D) from Lemma~. This establishes \|fracdcal Ldmu_(N)\|_F^2 le 4varepsilon^2 L/n le O(varepsilon^2 Ld/n) via Part~14, hence \|fracdcal Ldmu_(N)\|_F le O(varepsilonsqrtLd/n). Inductive step. Assume the claim for layer nu+1. We bound the auxiliary term G_(nu),p(t) (Part~3 of Lemma~). The factor kappa U_(nu)(t) Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)^top diag(1_n - frac12e_ell) (diagsigma - sigmasigma^top)Lambda_(nu-1),i(t) is bounded by: & ~ big\| kappa U_(nu)(t)Lambda_(nu-1), i (t)^top diag(1_n - tfrac12e_ell) (diagsigma_(nu), p(t) - sigma_(nu), p(t)sigma_(nu), p(t)^top)Lambda_(nu-1), i (t) big\|_F \\ leq & ~ kappa cdot \|U_(nu)(t)\|_F cdot \|Lambda_(nu-1),i(t)\|_F^2 cdot O(1) \\ leq & ~ kappa cdot O(dB) cdot O(L) cdot O(1) \\ = & ~ O(kappa L^2dB) leq O(L^2dB), where we use Parts 4 and 5, the fact that diagsigma - sigmasigma^top has spectral norm at most 1, and kappa = 1/sqrtm leq 1. To bound the random sum sum_rin[m] a_(nu),r(t)langlefracdcal Ldmu_(nu+1),p, a_(nu),r(t)rangle\, w_(nu),r(t)\,I\cdot\, we again apply Hoeffding at t=0 (where a_(nu),r,k(0)in\-1,+1\ is i.i.d.\ and independent of w_(nu),r(0)) to obtain \|G_(nu),p(0)\|_2^2 le omegacdot O(L^2 d^2.5 B^3), and then propagate to t>0 via the A-drift bound \|A_(nu)(t)-A_(nu)(0)\|_F le R_A from Lemma~ and the W-drift bound \|w_(nu),r(t)-w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le R from Part~9 of this lemma: \|G_(nu),p(t)\|_2 le \|G_(nu),p(0)\|_2 + O(omegasqrtm\,\|A_(nu)(t)-A_(nu)(0)\|_F + omegasqrtm d\,R) = O(sqrtomega cdot Ld^1.25B^1.5), so that \|G_(nu),p(t)\|_2^2 le omegacdot O(L^2 d^2.5B^3) le o(1) under Definition~'s choice omega = o(1/(NL^2 d^2.5B^3)) and the strengthened width of Lemma~. Therefore I_d + diag(G_(nu),p(t)) = (1pm o(1))I_d, and by Part~3 of Lemma~: Big\|fracdcal Ldmu_(nu),p(t)Big\|_2 = frac2varepsilonn\|(sf F_p(t)-sf Y_p)\|_2(1pm o(1)), which preserves the Theta(varepsilon^2cal L/n) per-layer scaling. Summing over pin[nL] (which produces a single factor of n from sum_p \|F_p-Y_p\|^2 = nL) and inducting: big\| fracd cal L(t, D)d mu_(nu)(t) big\|_F^2 asymp fracvarepsilon^2n cdot cal L(t, D). Proof of Part 16. We bound \|gamma_(nu),p(t)\|_2, where gamma_(nu),p(t) is the kernel feature for U_(nu). By the definition, the leading factor is fracomega kappasqrtm, multiplied by tensors of bounded norm (Part~5, Part~7) and a sum over r that is controlled by Hoeffding as in Part~15. Choosing kappa = 1/sqrtm as in Definition~, we have fracomegakappasqrtm = fracomegam, and the entire bound reduces to \| gamma_(nu),p(t)\|_2 leq o(1/sqrtm), completing the proof. This completes the proof of all parts of the lemma.

nodes.statement: Fix a layer nuin[N]. Conditioned on \U_(nu'), W_(nu'), A_(nu')\_nu'<nu, suppose the attention outputs \o_(nu),p(0)\_pin[nL]subset R^d satisfy: item[bf (P1)] (Bounded norms.) \|o_(nu),p(0)\|_2 = Theta(1) for all pin[nL] (which holds by Part~5 of Lemma~). item[bf (P2)] (Pairwise non-parallelism.) There exists a constant rho_nu > 0 such that, for all pne q, |langle widetilde o_(nu),p(0), widetilde o_(nu),q(0)rangle| leq 1 - rho_nu, where widetilde o := o/\|o\|_2. Equivalently, no two normalized attention outputs at layer nu are within angular distance arccos(1-rho_nu) of being parallel. Then, with probability at least 1-delta over the Gaussian initialization W_(nu)(0)sim cal N(0, I)^dtimes m alone, the kernel H_(nu)'(0)inR^nLtimes nL satisfies frac1omega\,lambda_minbig(H_(nu)'(0)big) \;ge\; c_0 cdot rho_nu, i.e., lambda_(nu) ge c_0 rho_nu, where c_0>0 is an absolute constant depending only on d and delta.

nodes.name: Proof sketch
nodes.statement: The kernel H_(nu),p,q'(0) = fracomega^2msum_rin[m] langle o_(nu),p(0), o_(nu),q(0)rangle\,I\w_(nu),r^top o_(nu),p > 0,\,w_(nu),r^top o_(nu),q > 0\ has expectation (as mtoinfty, with wsim cal N(0,I_d)): E[H_(nu),p,q'(0)/omega^2] = langle o_p, o_qranglecdotfracpi - arccos(langlewidetilde o_p,widetilde o_qrangle)2pi =: K_nu(p,q), which is exactly the arc-cosine kernel of citepcs09. By the standard argument of citep[Proposition 1]dzps19 (also citealpdllw19, os20), the population kernel K_nu on \o_(nu),p\_pin[nL] has lambda_min(K_nu) > 0 as long as no two points are parallel; quantitatively, lambda_min(K_nu) ge c_0rho_nu for an absolute c_0 citep[Lemma 3.1]dzps19. Concentration of the empirical kernel to its expectation follows from a standard matrix Chernoff bound citepsy19; with mge poly(n,L,1/rho_nu,1/delta) (already implied by Definition~), \|H_(nu)'(0)/omega - omegacdot K_nu\|_F le omega c_0rho_nu/2 with probability at least 1-delta. nodes.name: On the non-parallelism condition (P2)
nodes.statement: Condition (P2) is automatically satisfied, with high probability, in our setting: the inputs Xin cal X are RMSNormed so \|X_ell\|_2=Theta(1) (Section~); for nu=1, o_(1),p(0) is a softmax-weighted convex combination of the input tokens, hence inherits non-parallelism from the input distribution. For nuge 2, o_(nu),p(0) is the attention output of the previous layer, which is a generic non-degenerate function of \o_(nu-1),p(0)\_p; the only way (P2) fails is if a positive-measure subset of input sequences has identical layer-nu representations, which is an event of measure zero under any continuous data distribution. We therefore treat Assumption~ as a consequence of input non-degeneracy + the architecture, rather than an opaque assumption. A formal counterexample requires constructing an input distribution that places mass on ``collision'' configurations; we are not aware of any such pathology arising in practice.

nodes.statement: (i) Bound on the FFN drift. The gradient of the loss with respect to A_(nu) is fracd cal L(t,D)d A_(nu)(t) = sum_pin[nL] alpha_(nu), p(t)\,Big(fracd cal L(t,D)d mu_(nu),p(t)Big)^\!\!top in R^mtimes d. By the matrix-product Frobenius bound \|sum_p u_p v_p^top\|_F^2 le (sum_p \|u_p\|_2^2)(sum_p \|v_p\|_2^2), Part~15 of Lemma~ (sum_p \|dcal L/dmu_(nu),p\|_2^2 asymp varepsilon^2 cal L(t,D)) and the bound \|alpha_(nu),p(t)\|_2 leq O(omega) established in (ii) below: Big\|fracd cal Ld A_(nu)(t)Big\|_F^2 leq big(nLcdot O(omega^2)big)cdot Obig(varepsilon^2 cal L(t,D)big) = O(omega^2 nL)cdot varepsilon^2 cal L(t,D). By Theorem~, cal L(t,D) leq exp(-alphavarepsilon^2 t)cal L(0,D). Integrating along the gradient flow and using alpha = Theta(omegalambda N), cal L(0,D)leq O(Ld) (Part~14): \|A_(nu)(t) - A_(nu)(0)\|_F leq int_0^t O(omegasqrtnL)cdotvarepsilonsqrtcal L(s,D)\,d s leq fracO(omegasqrtnLcdot Ld)alphavarepsilon = OBig(fracsqrtnL^2dlambda NvarepsilonBig). For this to be le R_A := O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)), we need sqrt m le O(1/(omegasqrtnL^2d/varepsilon)), equivalently m le O(varepsilon^2/(omega^2 nL^2d)); note that this is an upper bound on m that we may always trade for the lower-bound condition by choosing varepsilon accordingly. Under the regime varepsilon = xi/sf N used throughout (Definition~, Theorem~), the strengthened width m = Omegabig(fracn^4 L^6 d^2 exp(Cd)omega^6 lambda^8 delta^4 N^4big) ensures the above bound is le R_A. This proves (i). (ii) Norm of the FFN tangent feature. We bound \|alpha_(nu),p(t)\|_2 in two steps: first at t=0 via the half-Gaussian moment (which is valid because w_(nu),r(0)simN(0,I_d) is independent of o_(nu),p(0) and of all other parameters), then for t>0 via Lipschitz continuity in (W, o). Step 1: t=0. For each rin[m], w_(nu),r(0)simN(0, I_d) is independent of the data o_(nu),p(0) (a deterministic function of the input and the initial sigma), so langle w_(nu),r(0), o_(nu),p(0)ranglesimN(0, \|o_(nu),p(0)\|_2^2) with \|o_(nu),p(0)\|_2 = Theta(1) by Part~5. The half-Gaussian moment E[phi(Z)^2] = E[Z^2]/2 = \|o\|_2^2/2 for ZsimN(0,\|o\|_2^2) together with concentration over r (Lemma~ applied to the i.i.d.\ bounded variables phi(langle w_r,orangle)^2 le \|w_r\|_2^2 \|o\|_2^2 le O(dB^2)): frac1msum_r=1^m phibig(langle w_(nu),r(0),o_(nu),p(0)ranglebig)^2 = frac\|o_(nu),p(0)\|_2^22pm OBig(sqrtfracdB^2 log(1/delta)mBig) = O(1) with probability at least 1-delta under the lemma's width condition. Hence \|alpha_(nu),p(0)\|_2^2 = fracomega^2msum_r=1^m phibig(langle w_(nu),r(0),o_(nu),p(0)ranglebig)^2 le O(omega^2), so \|alpha_(nu),p(0)\|_2 le O(omega). Step 2: extension from t=0 to t>0. The map (w_(nu),r, o_(nu),p) mapsto alpha_(nu),p,r = (omega/sqrt m)phi(langle w_(nu),r, o_(nu),prangle) is jointly Lipschitz with constants (omega/sqrt m)\|o_(nu),p\|_2 and (omega/sqrt m)\|w_(nu),r\|_2 respectively (since phi is 1-Lipschitz). Combining with Parts~3, 9, 13 of Lemma~ (so that \|w_(nu),r\|_2 le O(sqrt d B), \|w_(nu),r(t)-w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 le R, \|o_(nu),p(t)-o_(nu),p(0)\|_2 le O(sqrt L R)): \|alpha_(nu),p(t) - alpha_(nu),p(0)\|_2^2 &le fracomega^2msum_r=1^mbig(\|o_(nu),p(0)\|_2cdot R + \|w_(nu),r(t)\|_2cdot O(sqrt L R)big)^2 \\ &le fracomega^2mcdot mcdot Obig(R^2 + L d B^2 R^2big) = Obig(omega^2 L d B^2 R^2big). With R = O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)) and the strengthened width condition m = Omega(n^4 L^6 d^2exp(Cd)/(omega^6lambda^8delta^4 N^4)), this is o(omega^2). Therefore: \|alpha_(nu),p(t)\|_2 le \|alpha_(nu),p(0)\|_2 + \|alpha_(nu),p(t)-alpha_(nu),p(0)\|_2 = O(omega) + o(omega) = O(omega), which establishes Part~(ii). (iii) Augmented-kernel perturbation bound. We bound the drift big|langlealpha_p(t),alpha_q(t)rangle - langlealpha_p(0),alpha_q(0)ranglebig| by the same scheme as Lemma~ (Steps for Q_(nu),p,q,1, Q_(nu),p,q,2, Q_(nu),p,q,3). The dependence of alpha on w_(nu) and o_(nu),p is identical in form to that of beta_(nu),p in Lemma~, only with the post-activation features replacing the indicator features. Repeating the chain of bounds yields: big|langlealpha_p(t),alpha_q(t)rangle - langlealpha_p(0),alpha_q(0)ranglebig| leq Obig(omega^2big)cdot big( \|w_(nu),r(t) - w_(nu),r(0)\|_2 + \|o_p(t) - o_p(0)\|_2 big) leq Obig(omega^2 sqrt L Rbig), where the second step uses Parts~9 and~13 of Lemma~. Summing over (p,q)in[nL]^2: \|H_(nu)^aug(t) - H_(nu)^aug(0)\|_F leq \|H_(nu)(t)-H_(nu)(0)\|_F + nLcdot Obig(omega^2 sqrt L Rbig). The first term is le omegalambda/8 by Lemma~. The second term, with R = O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)), becomes O(omegasqrtnLcdot L/(sqrt m\,lambda N)); the strengthened width m = Omega(n^4 L^6 d^2 exp(Cd)/(omega^6lambda^8delta^4 N^4)) makes this le omegalambda/8. Combining and applying Fact~ yields lambda_min(H_(nu)^aug(t)otimes I_d)ge omegalambda/4.

nodes.name: Stop-time closure of the bootstrapping cycle
nodes.statement: The bounds in Lemma~ (kernel stability), Lemma~ (FFN drift), and Theorem~ (exponential loss decay) are proved conditional on each other through the per-step inequalities in Lemma~ (Parts~5,~9--13): kernel stability assumes the parameters stay inside the lazy ball; the lazy-ball drift bound R=O(1/(sqrt m\,omegalambda N)) assumes exponential loss decay; and exponential loss decay assumes kernel stability. To break this circularity without resorting to a literal substitution chain, we use the standard stopping-time argument of citep[Section 3]dzps19. Define the stopping time tau := inf\t ge 0 : \|theta(t)-theta(0)\|_F > R\ with R as above, and let E_t = \tau > t\ be the event that the trajectory has not exited the lazy ball by time t. On E_t all conclusions of Lemma~ and Lemma~ hold by construction; conditional on these, Theorem~ gives cal L(s, D) le exp(-alphavarepsilon^2 s)cal L(0,D) for all sle t. Integrating the gradient-flow drift on [0,t] with this exponentially decaying loss recovers \|theta(t)-theta(0)\|_F le R/2, contradicting tau le t. Hence tau = infty almost surely, the lazy ball is never exited, and the three results hold unconditionally for all tge 0. This is the precise sense in which the bootstrapping cycle in Figure~ closes.

{\bf Proof of Part 1.} We first note that the naive time complexity of matrix multiplication is $d_1d_2d_3$ for matrices $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_2 \times d_3}$. Formally, ${\sf Multiply}(A, B) = O(d_1d_2d_3)$.

    The following analysis follows from $v \in [N]$, $p \in [nL]$ and $i = \lfloor p / L \rfloor$.

    The complexity of ${\sf Multiply}(\Lambda_{(\nu-1), i}(t), U_{(\nu)}(t))$ is $O(Ld^2)$.

    The complexity of ${\sf Multiply}(\Lambda_{(\nu-1), i}(t) U_{(\nu)}(t), \Lambda_{(\nu-1), i}(t)^\top)$ is $O(L^2d)$.

    The complexity of naive softmax is $O(L^2)$.

    The complexity of ${\sf Multiply}(\Lambda_{(\nu-1), i}(t)^\top, \sigma_{(\nu), p}(t))$ is $O(Ld)$. Since the parallelization, total complexity should be $O(L^2d)$.

    The complexity of ${\sf Multiply}(  W_{(\nu)}(t))^\top , o_{(\nu), p}(t))$ is $O(Lmd)$.

    The complexity of ${\sf Multiply}(A_{(\nu)}^\top,(W_{(\nu)}(t))^\top o_{(\nu),p}(t)^\top)$ is the standard $O(Lmd)$ multiplications via real-valued multiplication, since $A_{(\nu)}$ is a trainable continuous matrix updated by gradient flow (Section~\ref{sec:preli}).

    Summing all complexity, we have the total complexity:
    \begin{align*}
        O(Ld^2 + L^2d+L^2+L^2d+Lmd+Lmd) \leq O(Lmd),
    \end{align*}
    where this step follows from $m$ is the major term.

nodes.name: Why the exponent has $1/\mathsf{N}$ rather than absorbing it
nodes.statement: The factor 1/N = 1/n in the exponent is essential: it traces directly to the average-loss convention L = frac1n\|F-Y\|_F^2 via Part~15 of Lemma~. We track this 1/N explicitly throughout, because N is one of the very scaling-law variables being analyzed and cannot be folded into a non-data ``constant''. Hiding this factor inside an absorbing constant ``alpha=Theta(lambda)'' would produce a phase boundary of CasympN^6 rather than the correct CasympN^7; the qualitative two-stage shape is preserved either way, but the polynomial scaling differs by one power of N.

\label{rem:n_in_rate}
The factor $1/\mathsf{N} = 1/n$ in the exponent is essential: it traces directly to the average-loss convention $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathsf{F}-\mathsf{Y}\|_F^2$ via Part~15 of Lemma~\ref{lem:helpful_bounds}. We track this $1/\mathsf{N}$ explicitly throughout, because $\mathsf{N}$ is one of the very scaling-law variables being analyzed and cannot be folded into a non-data ``constant''. Hiding this factor inside an absorbing constant ``$\alpha=\Theta(\lambda)$'' would produce a phase boundary of $\mathsf{C}\asymp\mathsf{N}^6$ rather than the correct $\mathsf{C}\asymp\mathsf{N}^7$; the qualitative two-stage shape is preserved either way, but the polynomial scaling differs by one power of $\mathsf{N}$.

nodes.statement: Proof of (n, |B|)-Fixed Convergence. We bound the per-step contribution of stochastic minibatching to the loss derivative, then combine with Lemma~ to obtain an exponential decay. From Lemma~ we have (with probability at least 1-delta), with the 1/n factor from Part~15: EBig[fracdd tcal L(t,D)Big] le -fracCcdotomegalambda Ncdot varepsilon^2ncdot cal L(t,D). The instantaneous fluctuation due to stochastic batching B(t) is controlled as follows. For any single per-sample gradient term, Lemma~ (Part 15) and the perturbation control of the kernel give: Big| fracd d t cal L(t, D) Big| leq OBig(varepsilon^2fracNsqrtmBig) cdot cal L(t, D), which arises from the bound \|fracd cal Ld mu_(nu)(t)\|^2_Fasymp varepsilon^2 cal L(t,D) summed over N layers, multiplied by the kernel norm \|H_(nu)(t)\|le O(1/sqrtm) uniformly under Definition~. Choosing m = Omega(n/(Nomegalambda)^2) as in Definition~, we get: Big| fracd d t cal L(t, D) Big| leq oBig(varepsilon^2 fracsqrt|B|sqrtnB omega lambda Big) cdot cal L(t, D), where |B| := min_tge 0 |B(t)| ge 1. By Lemma~ (Hoeffding's inequality applied to the empirical mean over a batch of size |B|), with probability at least 1-delta: & ~ Big| fracd d t cal L(t, D) - Ebig[fracd d t cal L(t, D)big] Big| \\ leq & ~ oBig(varepsilon^2fracsqrt|B|sqrtnB omega lambda Big) cdot sqrtfracn|B| log(1/delta)cdot cal L(t, D) \\ leq & ~ frac12C_1cdot varepsilon^2cdot cal L(t, D), where C_1 := Ccdot omegalambda N/n, the first step uses the per-sample bound and the variance reduction from a batch of size |B|, and the second step uses B = O(sqrtlog(Nmd/delta)) together with Definition~ so that the stochastic deviation is at most half of the deterministic decay. Combining with Equation~: fracd d t cal L(t, D) leq -frac12C_1cdot varepsilon^2 cdot cal L(t, D). Solving this scalar ODE inequality (Grönwall) yields: cal L(t, D) leq exp\!left(- fracCcdot varepsilon^2 omegalambda Ntnright) cdot cal L(0, D). Setting alpha := Ccdot omegalambda N as in Theorem~'s statement (we explicitly do not absorb the 1/n = 1/N factor into the constant, because N is a scaling-law variable; see Remark~). With t = sf T: cal L(sf T, D) leq exp\!left(- fracalpha cdot varepsilon^2 TNright) cdot cal L(0, D), as claimed. Equivalently, absorbing the omega N = poly(1/L,1/d,1/B) into a polynomial-in-(L,d,B) constant baralpha := Clambda gives the announced informal form.

nodes.statement: The strategy is: (a) construct an idealized infinite-width NTK predictor F^ntk, which is the kernel-regression solution against the target F^*, where the kernel is the transformer-specific layer-aggregated NTK K(x,y):=sum_nuin[N]H_(nu),x,y(0) (Section~), not the 2-layer ReLU NTK on prefix-mean-pooled inputs; (b) by the realizability assumption that F^* lies in the RKHS H_K of the layer-aggregated transformer NTK, F^ntk = F^* exactly within this RKHS; (c) apply the finite-width NTK approximation result of Theorem 3.2 in citepadh+19, lifted to multi-layer transformers via the matrix-to-vector reduction of Appendix~, to bound |F(X,theta(infty)) - F^ntk(X)|^2 leq varepsilon_app^2 where varepsilon_app>0 is the approximation target accuracy (a different parameter from the model scaling coefficient varepsilon; see Remark~ below). Remark on the choice of kernel: a simpler 2-layer-MLP-on-prefix-mean kernel predictor of the form F_ell^ntk,simp(X) = E_w[ReLU(langlefrac1ellsum_ell'leellX_ell', w(T)rangle)] + X_ell suffices for the approximation upper bound of Theorem~ when F^* is itself realizable in the prefix-MLP RKHS; we record this simpler form below. For the general case where F^* is realizable in the layer-aggregated transformer NTK H_K (which is a strictly larger RKHS), we use the transformer-NTK predictor F^ntk defined above. The bound inf\|F-F^*\|^2 le sf M^-2 holds in both settings; the transformer-NTK formulation is the more general realizability assumption. Step (a): Construct the kernel predictor. We construct the infinite-width transformer NTK predictor as the kernel-regression solution under the layer-aggregated kernel K(x,y) = sum_nuin[N]H_(nu),x,y(0) defined in Section~: F^ntk(X) := varepsilon cdot K(\X\,D_*)\,K(D_*,D_*)^-1\,widehat F^*(D_*) + X, where D_* ranges over a dense countable subset of cal X, K is evaluated on the layer-by-layer kernel features \beta_(nu),p(0), gamma_(nu),p(0)\ from Lemma~, and widehat F^* is the centred target F^*(X) - X_ell (the residual-connection adjustment, since the model output already contains the residual X_ell). The centred target is: widehat F^*_ell(cal A) := F^*_ell(cal A_1)^top - cal A_1, ell^top \\ F^*_ell(cal A_2)^top - cal A_2, ell^top \\ vdots \\ F^*_ell(cal A_|cal A|)^top - cal A_|cal A|, ell^top in R^|cal A| times d. For comparison and concreteness, we record the simplified prefix-MLP-only version that suffices when F^* is realizable in the simpler prefix-MLP RKHS: F_ell^ntk,simp(X) := & ~ lim_T to +infty varepsilon cdot E_w(0) sim cal N(0, I_d)left[ ReLU left( leftlangle frac1ell sum_ell'=1^ell X_ell', w(T) rightrangle right) right] + X_ell in R^d \\ = & ~ varepsilon cdot Big(cal K_ell(\ X\, cal X) cal K_ell(cal X, cal X)^-1 widehatF_ell(cal X) Big)^top, where cal K_ell(cdot,cdot) is the prefix-mean ReLU NTK kernel detailed below. This simplified form uses only the standard 2-layer ReLU NTK and is what the approximation argument of citepadh+19 directly bounds; in the general transformer case, the Gram matrix K above includes the additional gamma-features from softmax-attention (Lemma~, the U_(nu)-kernel piece) that distinguish transformer NTK from a prefix-MLP NTK. For reference, the simplified Gram matrix is: & ~ cal K_ell, i, j(cal A, cal B) \\ := & ~ left( frac1ell sum_ell'=1^ell cal A_i, ell'right)^top left( frac1ell sum_ell'=1^ell cal B_j, ell' right) cdot E_w sim cal N(0, I_d)left[I left\langle frac1ell sum_ell'=1^ell cal A_i, ell', w rangle > 0,\ langle frac1ell sum_ell'=1^ell cal B_j, ell', w rangle > 0 right\ right]. The centred target widehat F accounts for the residual connection: the model output already contains X_ell, so only F^*(X) - X_ell needs to be approximated by the kernel features. Step (b): Reduce approximation to RKHS interpolation. The approximation error is: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) E_(X, Y) sim cal Dbig[ \| F(X) - F^*(X)\|_F^2 big] = & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ leq & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^ntk\|_L^F(cal X)^2 + \| F^ntk - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ = & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^ntk\|_L^F(cal X)^2, where the first step rewrites the expectation as an L^F(cal X) norm, the second step is a triangle decomposition, and the third step uses F^ntk = F^* under the realizability assumption that F^* lies in the RKHS H_K of the layer-aggregated transformer NTK K = sum_nu H_(nu)(0). The realizability assumption is the analogue of the standard NTK-realizability assumption used in citepadh+19, dzps19; it is automatically satisfied if F^* is itself a transformer of the same architecture (with potentially different weights), and is broader than realizability in any single beta- or gamma-feature subspace. Step (c): Apply finite-width approximation. By Theorem 3.2 in citepadh+19, for any approximation target accuracy varepsilon_app > 0 (distinct from the model scaling varepsilon; see Remark~), taking m = Theta(poly(1/varepsilon_app)) yields, with probability at least 1-delta over theta(0): lim_sf T rightarrow inftyleft|F_ell, k(X, theta(sf T)) - F_ell, k^ntk(X) right|^2 leq varepsilon_app^2 for all Xin cal X,\, ellin[L],\, kin[d]. Summing over ellin[L] and kin[d]: lim_sf T to infty E_Xsim cal Dbig[ \| F(X, theta(sf T)) - F^ntk(X) \|_F^2 big] leq varepsilon_app^2. Combining with Step (b) and choosing varepsilon_app lesssim sf M^-1 (so that the per-coordinate target accuracy of the bound from citepadh+19 matches the desired sf M^-2 squared error after summing Ld coordinates): lim_sf T to infty inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) E_(X, Y) sim cal Dbig[ \| F(X) - F^*(X)\|_F^2 big] leq varepsilon_app^2 leq sf M^-2, which is the claim. We emphasize that varepsilon_app is a property of the function class, realized through the width m, and is decoupled from the model-scaling coefficient: the proof of Theorem~, which sets the model scaling to varepsilon = xi/sf N, does not invoke the specialization varepsilon_app lesssim sf M^-1 of this corollary, but the varepsilon-parametric form of the generalization bound (see Equation~).

The approximation error is: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) E_(X, Y) sim cal Dbig[ \| F(X) - F^*(X)\|_F^2 big] = & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ leq & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^ntk\|_L^F(cal X)^2 + \| F^ntk - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ = & ~ inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) \| F - F^ntk\|_L^F(cal X)^2, where the first step rewrites the expectation as an L^F(cal X) norm, the second step is a triangle decomposition, and the third step uses F^ntk = F^* under the realizability assumption that F^* lies in the RKHS H_K of the layer-aggregated transformer NTK K = sum_nu H_(nu)(0). The realizability assumption is the analogue of the standard NTK-realizability assumption used in citepadh+19, dzps19; it is automatically satisfied if F^* is itself a transformer of the same architecture (with potentially different weights), and is broader than realizability in any single beta- or gamma-feature subspace. Step (c): Apply finite-width approximation. By Theorem 3.2 in citepadh+19, for any approximation target accuracy varepsilon_app > 0 (distinct from the model scaling varepsilon; see Remark~), taking m = Theta(poly(1/varepsilon_app)) yields, with probability at least 1-delta over theta(0): lim_sf T rightarrow inftyleft|F_ell, k(X, theta(sf T)) - F_ell, k^ntk(X) right|^2 leq varepsilon_app^2 for all Xin cal X,\, ellin[L],\, kin[d]. Summing over ellin[L] and kin[d]: lim_sf T to infty E_Xsim cal Dbig[ \| F(X, theta(sf T)) - F^ntk(X) \|_F^2 big] leq varepsilon_app^2. Combining with Step (b) and choosing varepsilon_app lesssim sf M^-1 (so that the per-coordinate target accuracy of the bound from citepadh+19 matches the desired sf M^-2 squared error after summing Ld coordinates): lim_sf T to infty inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) E_(X, Y) sim cal Dbig[ \| F(X) - F^*(X)\|_F^2 big] leq varepsilon_app^2 leq sf M^-2, which is the claim. We emphasize that varepsilon_app is a property of the function class, realized through the width m, and is decoupled from the model-scaling coefficient: the proof of Theorem~, which sets the model scaling to varepsilon = xi/sf N, does not invoke the specialization varepsilon_app lesssim sf M^-1 of this corollary, but the varepsilon-parametric form of the generalization bound (see Equation~).

nodes.name: Two distinct uses of $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: The symbol varepsilon is used in two distinct senses in the kernel-NTK literature: (a) the model scaling coefficient varepsilon>0 that multiplies the residual sum varepsilonsum_nu mu_(nu) in our model definition (Equation~), used throughout to control the lazy-regime norm; (b) the approximation target accuracy varepsilon_app>0 that appears in the finite-width NTK approximation bound \|F-F^ntk\|^2levarepsilon_app^2 of citepadh+19. We disambiguate these by writing varepsilon for (a) and varepsilon_app for (b). The choice varepsilon_app lesssim sf M^-1 in Step (c) is the standard balance: setting m = Theta(poly(1/varepsilon_app)) as in citepadh+19 produces a width that is consistent with our m = Omega(N^3 cdot poly) from Definition~. The approximation bound inf\|F-F^*\|^2 le sf M^-2 holds with target accuracy varepsilon_app = sf M^-1 in the sense of citepadh+19, which is what enters the generalization bound of Theorem~.

nodes.statement: Within the scope of this subsection, we redefine the model class as cal F_sf M, N(D) := \F(cdot, theta) : theta in R^sf M\. That is, cal F_sf M, N(D) collects every realizable parameterization of the architecture (Equation~) of total parameter count sf M, rather than the closure of training trajectories. Consequently, the infimum inf_F in cal F_sf M, N(D) Delta cal R(F) corresponds to the empirical risk minimizer (ERM) over the parameter space, and the generalization bound below applies to the ERM directly via the standard nonparametric statistics tool of Lemma~. The approximation error of the ERM in this class is independently bounded through the RKHS construction in Corollary~; the bound is therefore not contingent on lim_sf T to infty and addresses the technical concern that the optimization endpoint and the ERM need not coincide.

By the definitions of cal R(cdot) and Deltacal R(cdot) (Section~) and the data model Y = F^*(X) + Xi: Deltacal R(F) = & ~ cal R(F) - cal R(F^*) notag \\ = & ~ E_(X, Y) sim cal Dleft[ \| F(X) - Y\|_F^2 - \| F^*(X) - Y\|_F^2 right] notag \\ = & ~ E_(X, Y) sim cal Dleft[ \| F(X) - F^*(X) - Xi\|_F^2 - \| Xi \|_F^2 right] notag \\ = & ~ E_(X, Y) sim cal Dleft[ \| F(X) - F^*(X) \|_F^2 - 2langle vec(F(X) - F^*(X)),vec(Xi)rangle + \|Xi\|_F^2 - \| Xi \|_F^2 right] notag \\ = & ~ E_(X, Y) sim cal Dleft[ \| F(X) - F^*(X) \|_F^2 right]notag \\ = & ~ \| F - F^* \|_L^F(cal X)^2, where the first step follows from the definitions of cal R and Delta cal R, the second step follows from Y = F^*(X) + Xi, the third step follows from simple algebras, the fourth step follows from the independence of X and Xi, E[Xi] = 0_L times d (and so E[langlevec(F(X) - F^*(X)),vec(Xi)rangle]=0), the fifth step follows from cancellation of the \|Xi\|_F^2 terms, the sixth step follows from the definition of the L^F(cal X) norm. Next, we bound the approximation term. nodes.statement: Let all pre-conditions hold as Corollary~ and choose varepsilon = Theta(xi/sf N). Then, with a probability at least 1 - delta, the following condition divides the scaling trend into two stages: sf C > fracsf N^7log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2. item Stage I (Compute-Starved Stage). If Equation~ does not hold, then there exist constants alpha,C,c_2',C_opt'>0 depending polynomially on (L,d,1/lambda,1/omega) such that: c_2'\,exp\!big(-C_opt'\, kappa_sf optcdot xi^2sf C/sf N^7big)cdotcal L(0,D) \;le\; inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) \;le\; C exp\!big(-alpha\, xi^2sf C/sf N^7big) cdot cal L(0, D), where kappa_sf optin[sqrtlambda/lambda_max,\,1] is a square-root-condition-number factor that distinguishes the upper from the lower bound (see Theorem~ and Remark~). item Stage II (Data-Limited Stage). nodes.statement: Let F = F(cdot, theta(sf T)) denote the optimizing function obtained from running gradient flow until time sf T, i.e. F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) in the sense of Definition~. Let F' in cal F_sf M, N(D) be the empirical risk minimizer over the (re-defined; see Remark~) parameter space. By the triangle inequality in L^F(cal X) norm: Delta cal R(F) leq & ~ \| F - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ leq & ~ left(\| F - F'\|_L^F(cal X) + \| F' - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)right)^2, where the first step follows from Equation~, the second step follows from the triangle inequality. We control the optimization term \|F-F'\|_L^F(cal X) via the kernel-stable gradient flow, carrying the 1/N factor of Theorem~ (Remark~) through the integration. Bounding the residual weight movement after time sf T: & ~ max_nuin [N] max_r in [m] \| w_(nu), r(sf T) - w_(nu), r(+infty) \|_2 notag \\ leq & ~ int_sf T^infty max_nuin [N]max_r in [m]Big\| fracd cal L(s, D)d w_(nu), r(s) Big\|_2 d s notag\\ leq & ~ int_sf T^infty varepsilon cdot sqrtcal L(s, D) d s notag\\ leq & ~ varepsilon int_sf T^infty expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 s2NBig) cdot sqrt cal L(0, D)d s \\ = & ~ frac2Nalpha varepsilon expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T2NBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D), where the first step follows from the gradient-flow update Equation~ and Cauchy--Schwarz, the second step from Part~15 of Lemma~, the third step from Theorem~ after taking square roots, and the last step is direct integration. Following Part 12 of Lemma~ (which transforms parameter-space distance into the L^F(cal X) functional distance) and the definition of F, we get: \| F - F'\|_L^F(cal X) leq & ~ minBig\ PexpBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T2NBig),\, O(1) Big\ cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) leq expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T4NBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D), P := frac2CLNalphavarepsilon, with the following bookkeeping. The O(1)cdotsqrtcal L(0,D) branch of the minimum is the crude bound: every F in the Good Model Class keeps its hidden states and outputs at the initialization scale (Parts~3 and~5 of Lemma~), so \|F-F'\|_L^F(cal X) = O(sqrtLd) = O(sqrtcal L(0,D)), the latter since cal L(0,D) = Omega(Ld) with high probability over the noise. The second inequality absorbs the polynomial prefactor P = poly(N, L, d, 1/xi, 1/lambda, 1/omega) into the exponent: for alphavarepsilon^2sf T/(2N) ge 2log P this is the standard absorption P e^-x le e^-x/2; for smaller sf T --- a burn-in window of the same order as the Stage-I/II boundary, up to the O(1) factor log P/log(sf NLd/xi^2) --- the displayed exponential is read together with the crude branch, i.e.\ the upper-bound prefactor of Theorem~ absorbs P inside the burn-in window, where the bound asserts no more than Deltacal R(F) = O(cal L(0,D)). We rename alpha/4 as alpha below. Combining with Theorem~ and Equation~ (using the statistical term Ldcdotxi^2/sf N): inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D sqrtDeltacal R(F) leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + sqrt4varepsilon^2 + Ld cdot OBig(fracxi^2sf N + xivarepsilonBig) \\ leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + 2varepsilon + OBig(fracxisf N^1/2 + (xivarepsilon)^1/2Big) \\ leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + OBig(fracxisf N^1/2 + (xivarepsilon)^1/2Big), where the second step uses sqrta+b leq sqrta+sqrtb for a,bgeq 0, and the third step absorbs the 2varepsilon summand into the O(cdot) since varepsilon = xi/sf N leq xi/sf N^1/2 in this regime. We square both sides of the previous bound to obtain a bound on Deltacal R(F) itself: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ 2exp\!left(-2alpha varepsilon^2 T/Nright) cdot cal L(0, D) + OBig(fracxi^2sf N + xivarepsilonBig), using (a+b)^2 le 2a^2 + 2b^2 and absorbing the constant 2 into the O(cdot) on the second summand; the 1/N in the exponent is the average-loss factor of Remark~. For any total computational resource sf C with dataset size sf N, we follow Definition~ to require sf M = Theta(sf N^3), and we choose varepsilon = xi/sf N. Substituting: xivarepsilon = xi^2/sf N and alpha varepsilon^2/N = alpha xi^2/sf N^3. Condition 1 (Compute-Starved Stage). When the optimization term exp(-2alphavarepsilon^2 T/N) dominates the statistical xi^2/N term, equivalently when: & ~ sf T le fracNlog(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)2alphavarepsilon^2 = fracsf N^3 log(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)2alpha xi^2, which using sf C = O(sf MTN) and sf M = sf N^3 translates into: sf C leq fracsf N^7log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2 up to constants, we have: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ C exp\!left(-alpha xi^2sf T/sf N^3right) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ = & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf MTNsf N^4sf MBig) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ leq & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf Csf N^4sf MBig) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ leq & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf Csf N^7Big) cdot cal L(0, D), where the second equality multiplies and divides by sf MN, the third inequality uses sf C = O(sf MTN) geq sf NTM/c for some constant c, and the fourth uses sf M le sf N^3 in the exponent. The constant C = poly(L, d, 1/lambda, 1/omega). Condition 2 (Data-Limited Stage). When sf T > sf N^3 log(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)/(2alphaxi^2), or equivalently: sf C = O(sf MTN) > fracsf Msf N^4log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2 iff sf C > fracsf N^7log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2, the optimization term decays faster than the statistical floor; the bound reduces to: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ OBig(fracxi^2sf N Big). We now optimize over sf N subject to the compute budget. The constraint is xi^-2\,sf N^7log(sf Ncdot Ld/xi^2) le sf C. Writing u := sf N^7/xi^2, this becomes: ulog(u^1/7 cdot xi^2/7 Ld) leq sf C, whose maximal solution satisfies (treating the slowly varying log factor via the Lambert W function W(cdot), which inverts zmapsto zlog z): u_max = OBig( fracsf CW(sf C/xi^12)Big), quadso sf N_max = OBig( fracsf Cxi^2W(sf C/xi^12) Big)^1/7. Substituting back: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ OBig(fracxi^2sf N_max Big) = xi^12/7 cdot Oleft( fracsf CW(sf C/xi^12) right)^-1/7 leq xi^12/7 cdot widetildeOleft( sf C right)^-1/7, where W(cdot) is the Lambert W function and widetilde O hides log sf C factors. The exponent -1/7 is a direct consequence of the 1/N factor in Theorem~.

By the triangle inequality in L^F(cal X) norm: Delta cal R(F) leq & ~ \| F - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2 \\ leq & ~ left(\| F - F'\|_L^F(cal X) + \| F' - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)right)^2, where the first step follows from Equation~, the second step follows from the triangle inequality. We control the optimization term \|F-F'\|_L^F(cal X) via the kernel-stable gradient flow, carrying the 1/N factor of Theorem~ (Remark~) through the integration. Bounding the residual weight movement after time sf T: & ~ max_nuin [N] max_r in [m] \| w_(nu), r(sf T) - w_(nu), r(+infty) \|_2 notag \\ leq & ~ int_sf T^infty max_nuin [N]max_r in [m]Big\| fracd cal L(s, D)d w_(nu), r(s) Big\|_2 d s notag\\ leq & ~ int_sf T^infty varepsilon cdot sqrtcal L(s, D) d s notag\\ leq & ~ varepsilon int_sf T^infty expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 s2NBig) cdot sqrt cal L(0, D)d s \\ = & ~ frac2Nalpha varepsilon expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T2NBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D), where the first step follows from the gradient-flow update Equation~ and Cauchy--Schwarz, the second step from Part~15 of Lemma~, the third step from Theorem~ after taking square roots, and the last step is direct integration. Following Part 12 of Lemma~ (which transforms parameter-space distance into the L^F(cal X) functional distance) and the definition of F, we get: \| F - F'\|_L^F(cal X) leq & ~ minBig\ PexpBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T2NBig),\, O(1) Big\ cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) leq expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 T4NBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D), P := frac2CLNalphavarepsilon, with the following bookkeeping. The O(1)cdotsqrtcal L(0,D) branch of the minimum is the crude bound: every F in the Good Model Class keeps its hidden states and outputs at the initialization scale (Parts~3 and~5 of Lemma~), so \|F-F'\|_L^F(cal X) = O(sqrtLd) = O(sqrtcal L(0,D)), the latter since cal L(0,D) = Omega(Ld) with high probability over the noise. The second inequality absorbs the polynomial prefactor P = poly(N, L, d, 1/xi, 1/lambda, 1/omega) into the exponent: for alphavarepsilon^2sf T/(2N) ge 2log P this is the standard absorption P e^-x le e^-x/2; for smaller sf T --- a burn-in window of the same order as the Stage-I/II boundary, up to the O(1) factor log P/log(sf NLd/xi^2) --- the displayed exponential is read together with the crude branch, i.e.\ the upper-bound prefactor of Theorem~ absorbs P inside the burn-in window, where the bound asserts no more than Deltacal R(F) = O(cal L(0,D)). We rename alpha/4 as alpha below. Combining with Theorem~ and Equation~ (using the statistical term Ldcdotxi^2/sf N): inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D sqrtDeltacal R(F) leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + sqrt4varepsilon^2 + Ld cdot OBig(fracxi^2sf N + xivarepsilonBig) \\ leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + 2varepsilon + OBig(fracxisf N^1/2 + (xivarepsilon)^1/2Big) \\ leq & ~ expBig(-fracalpha varepsilon^2 TNBig) cdot sqrtcal L(0, D) + OBig(fracxisf N^1/2 + (xivarepsilon)^1/2Big), where the second step uses sqrta+b leq sqrta+sqrtb for a,bgeq 0, and the third step absorbs the 2varepsilon summand into the O(cdot) since varepsilon = xi/sf N leq xi/sf N^1/2 in this regime. We square both sides of the previous bound to obtain a bound on Deltacal R(F) itself: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ 2exp\!left(-2alpha varepsilon^2 T/Nright) cdot cal L(0, D) + OBig(fracxi^2sf N + xivarepsilonBig), using (a+b)^2 le 2a^2 + 2b^2 and absorbing the constant 2 into the O(cdot) on the second summand; the 1/N in the exponent is the average-loss factor of Remark~. For any total computational resource sf C with dataset size sf N, we follow Definition~ to require sf M = Theta(sf N^3), and we choose varepsilon = xi/sf N. Substituting: xivarepsilon = xi^2/sf N and alpha varepsilon^2/N = alpha xi^2/sf N^3. Condition 1 (Compute-Starved Stage). When the optimization term exp(-2alphavarepsilon^2 T/N) dominates the statistical xi^2/N term, equivalently when: & ~ sf T le fracNlog(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)2alphavarepsilon^2 = fracsf N^3 log(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)2alpha xi^2, which using sf C = O(sf MTN) and sf M = sf N^3 translates into: sf C leq fracsf N^7log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2 up to constants, we have: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ C exp\!left(-alpha xi^2sf T/sf N^3right) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ = & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf MTNsf N^4sf MBig) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ leq & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf Csf N^4sf MBig) cdot cal L(0, D) \\ leq & ~ C expBig(-alpha xi^2 fracsf Csf N^7Big) cdot cal L(0, D), where the second equality multiplies and divides by sf MN, the third inequality uses sf C = O(sf MTN) geq sf NTM/c for some constant c, and the fourth uses sf M le sf N^3 in the exponent. The constant C = poly(L, d, 1/lambda, 1/omega). Condition 2 (Data-Limited Stage). When sf T > sf N^3 log(sf Ncdot Ld /xi^2)/(2alphaxi^2), or equivalently: sf C = O(sf MTN) > fracsf Msf N^4log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2 iff sf C > fracsf N^7log( sf N cdot Ld/xi^2)xi^2, the optimization term decays faster than the statistical floor; the bound reduces to: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ OBig(fracxi^2sf N Big). We now optimize over sf N subject to the compute budget. The constraint is xi^-2\,sf N^7log(sf Ncdot Ld/xi^2) le sf C. Writing u := sf N^7/xi^2, this becomes: ulog(u^1/7 cdot xi^2/7 Ld) leq sf C, whose maximal solution satisfies (treating the slowly varying log factor via the Lambert W function W(cdot), which inverts zmapsto zlog z): u_max = OBig( fracsf CW(sf C/xi^12)Big), quadso sf N_max = OBig( fracsf Cxi^2W(sf C/xi^12) Big)^1/7. Substituting back: inf_F in cal F_sf M, T, N(D) sup_D in cal D Deltacal R(F) leq & ~ OBig(fracxi^2sf N_max Big) = xi^12/7 cdot Oleft( fracsf CW(sf C/xi^12) right)^-1/7 leq xi^12/7 cdot widetildeOleft( sf C right)^-1/7, where W(cdot) is the Lambert W function and widetilde O hides log sf C factors. The exponent -1/7 is a direct consequence of the 1/N factor in Theorem~.

Define the two-point family: F_0^* := 0, F_1^* := rho cdot g, rho := sqrtfracxi^22sf N. Both lie in cal H_K. Step 2: Bound the KL divergence. Under each F_j^*, the data law is D_j = cal Xtimes N(F_j^*(X), xi^2 I_Ld), so the per-sample KL divergence is D_KL(cal D_0\|cal D_1) = E_XBig[frac12xi^2\|F_0^*(X) - F_1^*(X)\|_F^2Big] = fracrho^22xi^2 cdot \|g\|_L^F(cal X)^2 = fracrho^22xi^2. For an i.i.d.\ dataset of size sf N, D_KL(cal D_0^otimes sf N\|cal D_1^otimes sf N) = sf Ncdot rho^2/(2xi^2). With our choice rho^2 = xi^2/(2sf N), we have: D_KL(cal D_0^otimes sf N\|cal D_1^otimes sf N) = frac14 le log 2. Step 3: Apply Le Cam's two-point lemma (Theorem 2.2 of citealptsy09). For any estimator widehat F: inf_widehat Fsup_jin\0,1\ E_Dsim cal D_j^otimessf Nbig[\|widehat F-F_j^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2big] ge frac14big(1-sqrtD_KL/2big)cdot \|F_0^*-F_1^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2. Substituting the bound on KL: inf_widehat Fsup_jin\0,1\ Ebig[\|widehat F-F_j^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2big] ge frac14big(1 - sqrt1/8big)cdot rho^2 ge frac18cdot fracxi^22sf N = fracxi^216sf N. Step 4: Translate to excess risk. By Equation~, Deltacal R(F) = \|F - F^*\|_L^F(cal X)^2, so: inf_widehat Fsup_F^*incal H_K Ebig[Deltacal R(widehat F)big] ge inf_widehat Fsup_jin\0,1\ Ebig[Deltacal R(widehat F)big] ge fracxi^216sf N, yielding the claim with c_1 = 1/16.
